content: Acute respiratory infections (ARIs) are a major cause of illness and death in children under five years of age, particularly in developing countries. When children with severe pneumonia require hospitalization, the standard treatment often involves the use of parenteral (injectable) antibiotics if a bacterial infection is suspected. However, this approach has several drawbacks. Parenteral antibiotics can cause significant pain and discomfort for children, which may lead to refusal of treatment or poor adherence. Additionally, the use of needles carries risks of complications, and in some healthcare settings, the necessary equipment for administering parenteral antibiotics may be unavailable. This can result in the need to transfer the child to another facility, increasing both the risks to the child and the overall cost of care. The objective of this study was to evaluate whether oral antibiotics are as effective and safe as parenteral antibiotics for treating severe pneumonia in children aged three months to five years. To address this question, a systematic search was conducted using databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, and LILACS, covering studies published up to July 2005. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that compared oral antibiotic therapy with parenteral antibiotic therapy in this population. Out of more than 1300 titles identified, only three studies met the eligibility criteria for inclusion in the review. One of these studies had not yet published its results at the time of the review. Due to differences in the therapies compared across the included studies, a meta-analysis was not performed. The first study, conducted by Campbell in 1988, compared oral co-trimoxazole with intramuscular procaine penicillin followed by oral ampicillin in 134 children. At the seventh day of follow-up, treatment failure was observed in 6 out of 66 children (9.1%) in the oral co-trimoxazole group and in 7 out of 68 children (10.2%) in the group receiving the combined treatment. The calculated risk difference was -0.01% (95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.11 to 0.09), indicating no significant difference between the two groups. The second study, conducted by the APPIS Group in 2004, involved 1702 children and compared oral amoxicillin with intravenous penicillin administered for two days, followed by oral amoxicillin. After 48 hours, treatment failure occurred in 161 out of 845 children (19%) in the oral amoxicillin group and in 167 out of 857 children (19%) in the parenteral penicillin group. The risk difference was -0.4% (95% CI: -4.2 to 3.3), again showing no significant difference between the two treatment approaches. The authors of this study also reported similar recovery rates in both groups at five and fourteen days. Based on the available evidence, the authors concluded that oral antibiotic therapy is a safe and effective alternative to parenteral antibiotics for hospitalized children with severe pneumonia, provided that the children do not exhibit any serious signs or symptoms.
